text: He who has hurt you must be either stronger or weaker than yourself. If he be weaker, spare him: if he be stronger, spare yourself.
plain: If they are weaker, go easy on them. If they are stronger, protect yourself. Either way, skip the fight.

text: That cannot be a great mind which is disturbed by injury.
plain: Being rattled by a slight shows how small the mind is.

text: How far more glorious is it to throw back all wrongs and insults from oneself, like one wearing armour of proof against all weapons, for revenge is an admission that we have been hurt.
plain: Hitting back proves the insult landed. Let it bounce off instead.

text: As weapons rebound from a hard surface, and solid substances hurt those who strike them, so also no insult can make a really great mind sensible of its presence, being weaker than that against which it is aimed.
plain: Insults only stick to a mind that is softer than the insult.

text: Anger brings grief to a father, divorce to a husband, hatred to a magistrate, failure to a candidate for office.
plain: Anger costs you your family, your standing and your shot at the thing you want.

text: Avarice scrapes together and amasses riches for some better man to use: anger spends money; few can indulge in it for nothing.
plain: Greed at least saves money. Rage burns it.

text: It is worse than luxury, because luxury enjoys its own pleasure, while anger enjoys another’s pain.
plain: Indulgence feeds on your own pleasure. Rage feeds on someone else's pain.

text: There is no greater proof of magnanimity than that nothing which befalls you should be able to move you to anger.
plain: Real strength is being unmoved by whatever happens to you.

text: We shall find much profit in that sound maxim of Democritus which defines peace of mind to consist in not labouring much, or too much for our strength, either in public or private matters.
plain: Peace of mind comes from not taking on more than you can carry.

text: Whenever you would attempt anything, first form an estimate both of your own powers, of the extent of the matter which you are undertaking, and of the means by which you are to accomplish it: for if you have to abandon your work when it is half done, the disappointment will sour your temper.
plain: Size up the job and your tools before you start, or quitting halfway will sour you.

text: Let our undertakings, therefore, be neither petty nor yet presumptuous and reckless: let our hopes not range far from home: let us attempt nothing which if we succeed will make us astonished at our success.
plain: Aim high, but not so high that success would shock you.

text: A dispute nourishes itself as it proceeds, and takes hold of those who plunge too deeply into it: it is easier to stand aloof than to extricate oneself from a struggle.
plain: Arguments feed themselves. Stay out of them early because getting out later is hard.

text: It is useful for a man to understand his disease, and to break its strength before it becomes developed.
plain: Know your own weakness and catch it while it is still small.

text: People do not all take offence in the same way; you ought then to know what your own weak point is, that you may guard it with especial care.
plain: Everyone has a trigger. Find yours and guard it.

text: Would you not be irascible? then be not inquisitive.
plain: If you don't want to be angry, stop digging for what people say about you.

text: A large part of mankind manufacture their own grievances either by entertaining unfounded suspicions or by exaggerating trifles.
plain: Most of our grievances are ones we built ourselves out of guesses and small stuff.

text: Anger often comes to us, but we often go to it. It ought never to be sent for: even when it falls in our way it ought to be flung aside.
plain: Anger finds you sometimes, but mostly you walk to it. Don't go looking.

text: If you want to find out the truth about anything, commit the task to time: nothing can be accurately discerned at a time of disturbance.
plain: You can't see clearly while you're worked up. Give it time first.

text: While you are angry, you ought not to be allowed to do anything.
plain: Don't act while you're angry. Not one thing.

text: Fight hard with yourself and if you cannot conquer anger, do not let it conquer you: you have begun to get the better of it if it does not show itself, if it is not given vent.
plain: If you can't kill the anger, at least don't let it out. Not showing it is the first win.

text: Our inward thoughts gradually become influenced by our outward demeanour.
plain: Act calm and the mind follows.

text: No yoke is so grievous as not to hurt him who struggles against it more than him who yields to it: the only way to alleviate great evils is to endure them and to submit to do what they compel.
plain: Fighting a burden hurts more than carrying it. Stop struggling and the weight eases.

text: The other vices move our minds; anger hurls them headlong.
plain: Most vices nudge you. Anger throws you.

text: There is no passion that is more frantic, more destructive to its own self; it is arrogant if successful, and frantic if it fails.
plain: Anger is cocky when it wins and frantic when it loses. It never comes out well.

text: Other passions gain a footing in the mind by slow degrees: anger’s conquest is sudden and complete, and, moreover, it makes all other passions subservient to itself.
plain: Other urges creep in. Anger takes over in a second and then runs everything else.

text: The man who is not angry remains unshaken by injury: he who is angry has been moved by it.
plain: Staying calm shows you weren't moved. Anger shows you were.

text: You say, “I cannot endure it: injuries are hard to bear.” You lie; for how can any one not be able to bear injury, if he can bear to be angry?
plain: If you can stand being furious, you can stand the insult. It's the easier of the two.

text: Let us therefore be more gentle one to another: we are bad men, living among bad men: there is only one thing which can afford us peace, and that is to agree to forgive one another.
plain: Everyone is flawed. The only way to peace is to forgive each other.

text: How far better is it to heal an injury than to avenge it? Revenge takes up much time, and throws itself in the way of many injuries while it is smarting under one.
plain: Revenge eats time and invites more trouble. Healing is cheaper.

text: We all retain our anger longer than we feel our hurt: how far better it were to take the opposite course and not meet one mischief by another.
plain: The hurt fades faster than the grudge. Don't answer one mess with another.

text: Have I less than I hoped for? well, perhaps I hoped for more than I ought.
plain: Feeling shorted? Maybe you expected too much.

text: A man will never be well off to whom it is a torture to see any one better off than himself.
plain: If someone else's success hurts you, you will never feel like you have enough.

text: Do you ask, what is your greatest fault? It is, that you keep your accounts wrongly: you set a high value upon what you give, and a low one upon what you receive.
plain: You overvalue what you give and undervalue what you get.

text: Believe me, the things which cause us such great heat are trifles, the sort of things that children fight and squabble over: there is nothing serious, nothing important in all that we do with such gloomy faces.
plain: Most of what we fight over is kid stuff. Lighten up.

text: A narrow path causes quarrels among those who pass up and down it; a wide and broadly spread road may be used by whole tribes without jostling.
plain: Fight over small scraps and you clash. Aim at something wide and there's room for everyone.

text: What bad habit of yours have you cured to-day? what vice have you checked? in what respect are you better?
plain: Ask it every night: what did I fix, what did I resist, how am I better?

text: A good man delights in receiving advice: all the worst men are the most impatient of guidance.
plain: Good people want feedback. Fools hate it.

text: The mind is strong enough to bear those evils for which it is prepared.
plain: You can handle what you saw coming. So expect trouble.

text: To reprove a man when he is angry is to add to his anger by being angry oneself.
plain: Yelling at an angry person just doubles the fire.

text: Let us set our own conscience fully at rest, but make no efforts to gain credit for ourselves: so long as we deserve well, let us be satisfied, even if we should be ill spoken of.
plain: Live clean, do good work, and let them talk.

text: Let us not moderate anger, but get rid of it altogether: what can moderation have to do with an evil habit?
plain: Don't manage a bad habit. Cut it out.

text: Life is a matter which does not admit of waste, and we have no spare time to throw away.
plain: Life can't be wasted. There's no spare time.

text: The time which you have marked for the death of another perhaps includes your own.
plain: The day you wish on your enemy may cover you too.

text: Wait but a little while. See, here comes death, who will make you all equals.
plain: Death levels everyone soon enough. Hold on.

text: Let us keep our tempers in spite of losses, wrongs, abuse or sarcasm, and let us endure with magnanimity our shortlived troubles: while we are considering what is due to ourselves, as the saying is, and worrying ourselves, death will be upon us.
plain: Stay level through losses and slights. Death is closing in while you stew.

text: Nothing, therefore, is more important than that we should not, like sheep, follow the flock that has gone before us, and thus proceed not whither we ought, but whither the rest are going.
plain: Don't follow the herd just because it's moving. Pick your own direction.

text: Let us therefore inquire, not what is most commonly done, but what is best for us to do, and what will establish us in the possession of undying happiness, not what is approved of by the vulgar, the worst possible exponents of truth.
plain: Do what is best, not what is popular. The crowd is a bad judge.

text: The happy man, therefore, is he who can make a right judgment in all things: he is happy who in his present circumstances, whatever they may be, is satisfied and on friendly terms with the conditions of his life.
plain: Happy means seeing clearly and being at peace with where you are.

text: A man should be unbiassed and not to be conquered by external things: he ought to admire himself alone, to feel confidence in his own spirit, and so to order his life as to be ready alike for good or for bad fortune.
plain: Trust yourself and stay ready for good luck or bad.

text: You may, then, boldly declare that the highest good is singleness of mind: for where agreement and unity are, there must the virtues be: it is the vices that are at war one with another.
plain: Being whole, with no inner war, is the goal.

text: Why do you talk of pleasures to me? I am seeking to find what is good for man, not for his belly; why, cattle and whales have larger ones than he.
plain: I want what's good for a person, not for his stomach. Cattle have bigger ones.

text: You devote yourself to pleasures, I check them; you indulge in pleasure, I use it; you think that it is the highest good, I do not even think it to be good: for the sake of pleasure I do nothing, you do everything.
plain: You chase pleasure. I keep it on a leash.

text: Let virtue lead the way and bear the standard: we shall have pleasure for all that, but we shall be her masters and controllers; she may win some concessions from us, but will not force us to do anything.
plain: Enjoy things, but on your terms. Pleasure takes orders, not gives them.

text: Let us bear with magnanimity whatever the system of the universe makes it needful for us to bear: we are all bound by this oath: “To bear the ills of mortal life, and to submit with a good grace to what we cannot avoid.”
plain: Accept what you can't avoid with grace.

text: You do not afford virtue a solid immoveable base if you bid it stand on what is unsteady: and what can be so unsteady as dependence on mere chance, and the vicissitudes of the body and of those things which act on the body?
plain: Build on what you control, not luck or your body's moods.

text: I am not a wise man, and I will not be one in order to feed your spite: so do not require me to be on a level with the best of men, but merely to be better than the worst: I am satisfied, if every day I take away something from my vices and correct my faults.
plain: Don't expect perfect. Just be a little better each day than the worst, and keep trimming.

text: I’ve lived, I’ve run the race which Fortune set me.
plain: Finish your race so you can say this at the end.

text: Men deserve praise for engaging in profitable studies, even though they stop short of producing any results.
plain: Trying to learn and improve counts, even if it doesn't pay off yet.

text: I will do nothing because of public opinion, but everything because of conscience: whenever I do anything alone by myself I will believe that the eyes of the Roman people are upon me while I do it.
plain: Act as if watched even when alone, and answer to your conscience rather than the crowd.

text: So croak away, and exercise your miserable tongues in reproaching good men: open wide your jaws, bite hard: you will break many teeth before you make any impression.
plain: Haters wear themselves out on you. Let them bite.

text: In fine, my riches belong to me, you belong to your riches.
plain: Own your stuff or it owns you.

text: As he is capable of performing a journey upon his own feet, but yet would prefer to mount a carriage, just so he will be capable of being poor, yet will wish to be rich; he will own wealth, but will view it as an uncertain possession which will some day fly away from him.
plain: You can be fine without money, enjoy it when you have it, and know it can vanish.

text: All the difference in the world: for riches are slaves in the house of a wise man, but masters in that of a fool.
plain: Money serves the wise and masters the fool.

text: The hardness of flint is known to none so well as to those who strike it.
plain: Whoever attacks you learns how hard you are.

text: I offer myself to all attacks, like some lonely rock in a shallow sea, which the waves never cease to beat upon from whatever quarter they may come, but which they cannot thereby move from its place nor yet wear away, for however many years they may unceasingly dash against it.
plain: Be the rock in the waves. Hits don't move you.
